cues.en: All right.
In this section we are going to learn about dynamic programming.
Now what is dynamic programming now?
By definition, it is a problem solving technique to solve the problems by breaking them into the smaller
and overlapping subproblems.
Now to understand this definition, let's use real life example.
So let's say we want to solve this math question.
So we have a seven ones over here.
And we are summing up them.
It's obvious that if the sum of them is going to be seven.
Now let's say we have another problem like this where we have the seven ones plus two.
So in this case we have already calculated this sum of the seven ones which is seven.
So in case of dynamic programming, we don't need to calculate this again because we have already calculated
it and we have saved it somewhere in the memory.
So we can use it to calculate the new problem.
In terms of optimization, this is faster than the way that we calculate it.
Again.
So this is the smart way of solving the problems like this.
So in case of dynamic programming.
We don't do the same thing twice.
So when we calculate the problem, we are solving it.
And if we encounter the same problem instead of solving it, we simply use the answer that we got before.
So the logic is when we break the main problem into subproblems, we see that we have a smaller problem
which is coming again and again.
So instead of solving it again, we solve it once and store the answer for the next term.
So the next time when we encounter the same problem, we simply use the previous solution.
So if we compare the dynamic programming with the divide and conquer algorithms, we can see that it's
the optimization of divide and conquer algorithm.
In case of divide and conquer algorithms, we divide the main problem into subproblems and we solve
the subproblems and combine them.
So this is applicable for dynamic programming.
Also we are doing the same thing dividing the main problem into subproblems, then solving the subproblems
and combining them together to get the solution to the main problem.
But here the main difference is that we are not solving the same subproblems twice.
So the main property of dynamic programming is overlapping subproblems.
We have said that to be able to calculate the big problem, we are dividing it to the subproblems.
And if finding two solution to the big problem involves the solving the same subproblems, it means
that we have an overlapping subproblem so we can save them and use it for future.
So one of the example for this one can be the Fibonacci series.
So let's say we are calculating the Fibonacci for and we know that this is the sum of the previous Fibonacci
which is three and two.
Then we can calculate the two which is going to be two and one.
And then we can calculate two which is going to be one and zero.
So as you can see I have colored the repetitive values in the same color.
So here we have already calculated Fibonacci two.
So we don't need to calculate it one more time.
Or we calculated the Fibonacci one.
We don't need to calculate it one more time.
So we are going to save it and use it in the memory.
So there are two different methods of dynamic programming for solving the problem.
The first one is top down with memoization and the second one is bottom up with tabulation.
So let's look at them in the next lecture.
